summary.text: Admissibility forces the last entry to be either $1$ or, if larger, exactly $2$ with penultimate entry $1$. According as the preceding prefix contains $1$ (in the first case) or $2$ (in the second), deleting the suffix and either leaving the prefix unchanged or subtracting $1$ or $2$ partitions the objects into four disjoint reversible classes, giving the recurrence $b_N=2b_{N-1}+2b_{N-2}$ with initial counts $1,3$.

full_proof.text:
Let an admissible sequence of length \(N\) mean a sequence
\[
 x=(x_1,x_2,\ldots,x_N)
\]
of positive integers satisfying the following two conditions.

1. If \(M=\max_i x_i\), then every integer in the interval \(\{1,2,\ldots,M\}\) occurs among the entries of \(x\). This is the condition that the sequence covers an initial interval of positive integers.

2. Whenever \(i<j\) and \(j\ne i+1\), equivalently whenever \(j\ge i+2\), one has
\[
 x_i\ge x_j.
\]
Thus every pair of parts in nonconsecutive positions is weakly decreasing from left to right.

Write \(B_N\) for the set of admissible sequences of length \(N\), and let \(b_N=|B_N|\). These sets are finite: if an admissible sequence has maximum \(M\), then the \(M\) distinct values \(1,2,\ldots,M\) must all occur in its \(N\) positions, so \(M\le N\). Hence every entry belongs to \(\{1,\ldots,N\}\), leaving only finitely many possible sequences.

We will prove
\[
 b_1=1,\qquad b_2=3,
\]
and, for every \(N\ge3\),
\[
 b_N=2b_{N-1}+2b_{N-2}. \tag{1}
\]
This will identify \(b_{n+1}\) with A028859.

First observe that every admissible sequence contains a \(1\). Indeed, its maximum is at least \(1\), since all entries are positive, and the initial-interval condition therefore requires the value \(1\) to occur.

For the initial values, an admissible sequence of length one must be \((1)\). To see this, if its sole entry were \(m>1\), it could not also contain all of \(1,\ldots,m-1\). Thus
\[
 b_1=1.
\]
For length two, the non-adjacent condition imposes no restriction, because the two positions are adjacent. The initial-interval condition allows exactly
\[
 (1,1),\qquad (1,2),\qquad (2,1).
\]
There cannot be a maximum at least \(3\), since three distinct required values could not fit into two positions. Hence
\[
 b_2=3.
\]

We next give four constructions that produce every admissible sequence of length \(N\ge3\). If \(u=(u_1,\ldots,u_r)\), write \(u+c\) for \((u_1+c,\ldots,u_r+c)\). For \(N\ge3\), define the following maps:
\[
\begin{aligned}
 A:B_{N-1}&\longrightarrow B_N,
 &A(u)&=(u_1,\ldots,u_{N-1},1),\\
 B:B_{N-1}&\longrightarrow B_N,
 &B(u)&=(u_1+1,\ldots,u_{N-1}+1,1),\\
 C:B_{N-2}&\longrightarrow B_N,
 &C(v)&=(v_1+1,\ldots,v_{N-2}+1,1,2),\\
 D:B_{N-2}&\longrightarrow B_N,
 &D(v)&=(v_1+2,\ldots,v_{N-2}+2,1,2).
\end{aligned} \tag{2}
\]

We first check carefully that these constructions really do produce admissible sequences.

For \(A(u)\), positivity is immediate. If the maximum of \(u\) is \(m\), the appended \(1\) does not change the maximum, and \(u\) already contains every value from \(1\) through \(m\). Thus the initial-interval condition is preserved. The required inequalities between positions already belonging to \(u\) hold because \(u\) is admissible. If a position in \(u\) is non-adjacent to the new last position, its value is positive and hence at least the new last value \(1\). Therefore \(A(u)\) is admissible.

For \(B(u)\), if \(u\) has maximum \(m\), then the shifted prefix \(u+1\) contains all the values \(2,3,\ldots,m+1\), and the appended final entry supplies \(1\). Thus the resulting sequence covers exactly the initial interval through its maximum \(m+1\). Shifting all entries of the prefix by the same amount preserves every weak inequality inside the prefix. Every prefix entry is at least \(2\), so every required comparison with the final \(1\) also holds. Hence \(B(u)\) is admissible.

For \(C(v)\), let the maximum of \(v\) be \(m\). The sequence \(v\) contains every value \(1,\ldots,m\), so the shifted prefix \(v+1\) contains every value \(2,\ldots,m+1\). The appended entries \(1,2\) supply \(1\) (and another occurrence of \(2\)), so the whole sequence covers \(1,\ldots,m+1\), which is precisely the interval through its maximum. Inequalities within the shifted prefix are inherited from \(v\). Every shifted prefix entry is at least \(2\). Consequently it is at least the penultimate entry \(1\), and it is also at least the final entry \(2\), whenever the relevant positions are non-adjacent. The last two entries \(1,2\) are adjacent, so no inequality is required between them. Thus \(C(v)\) is admissible.

The same argument applies to \(D(v)\). The shifted prefix \(v+2\) contains all values \(3,4,\ldots,m+2\), while the suffix \((1,2)\) supplies the two missing smallest values. Hence the sequence covers \(1,\ldots,m+2\). All inequalities within the prefix are preserved by the shift. Prefix entries are at least \(3\), so all required comparisons with either \(1\) or \(2\) hold, and again the adjacent pair \((1,2)\) need not be weakly decreasing. Therefore \(D(v)\) is admissible.

All four maps in (2) are injective: one recovers the source by deleting the appended suffix and then, in cases \(B,C,D\), subtracting the indicated constant from every remaining entry.

We now prove that these four images are disjoint and exhaust \(B_N\). Let
\[
 x=(x_1,\ldots,x_N)\in B_N,
\]
where \(N\ge3\).

First suppose that \(x_N=1\). Put
\[
 p=(x_1,\ldots,x_{N-1}).
\]
There are two cases.

If \(p\) contains a \(1\), then \(p\) is itself admissible. Positivity and all its non-adjacent inequalities are inherited from \(x\). Its maximum is the same as the maximum of \(x\), because the omitted final value \(1\) still occurs in \(p\), and every value required by the covering condition for \(x\) still occurs in \(p\): for values greater than \(1\), an occurrence cannot have been the deleted final entry, while for the value \(1\) we are assuming another occurrence in \(p\). Thus \(p\in B_{N-1}\), and
\[
 x=A(p).
\]

If \(p\) does not contain a \(1\), all of its entries are at least \(2\). Define
\[
 u=(x_1-1,\ldots,x_{N-1}-1).
\]
Then \(u\) has positive entries. If the maximum of \(p\) is \(M\), the maximum of \(u\) is \(M-1\). For every \(k\) with \(1\le k\le M-1\), the value \(k+1\) lies between \(2\) and \(M\), so the covering condition for \(x\) gives an occurrence of \(k+1\). This occurrence is in \(p\), since the deleted last entry is \(1\). Subtracting \(1\) gives an occurrence of \(k\) in \(u\). Thus \(u\) covers its initial interval. Subtracting the same number from every entry preserves all weak inequalities, so \(u\in B_{N-1}\). We then have
\[
 x=B(u).
\]

This completely handles sequences ending in \(1\). Moreover, the two subcases are disjoint: the prefix of every sequence in the image of \(A\) contains a \(1\), because every admissible source contains a \(1\), whereas every entry of the prefix of a sequence in the image of \(B\) is at least \(2\).

It remains to consider the case
\[
 x_N\ge2. \tag{3}
\]
We claim first that
\[
 x_{N-1}=1. \tag{4}
\]
For every \(i\le N-2\), positions \(i\) and \(N\) are non-adjacent, so admissibility gives
\[
 x_i\ge x_N\ge2.
\]
Thus none of \(x_1,\ldots,x_{N-2}\) is \(1\). The final entry is not \(1\) by (3). But every admissible sequence must contain \(1\), so the only remaining possible position for it is \(N-1\), proving (4).

We next claim that in fact
\[
 x_N=2. \tag{5}
\]
If instead \(x_N\ge3\), then the same non-adjacent comparisons would show that every \(x_i\) with \(i\le N-2\) is at least \(3\). The penultimate entry is \(1\), and the final entry is at least \(3\). Hence the value \(2\) would occur nowhere in the sequence. This contradicts the initial-interval condition, since a sequence whose maximum is at least \(3\) must contain \(2\). This proves (5).

Consequently every admissible sequence not ending in \(1\) has suffix exactly \((1,2)\). Let
\[
 q=(x_1,\ldots,x_{N-2})
\]
be the prefix before this suffix. Since each position in \(q\) is non-adjacent to the final position, (5) implies that every entry of \(q\) is at least \(2\). Again there are two cases.

Suppose first that \(q\) contains a \(2\). Define
\[
 v=(x_1-1,\ldots,x_{N-2}-1).
\]
This is positive. Let \(M\) be the maximum of \(x\). The maximum is already attained in \(q\): all entries of \(q\) are at least \(2\), and the assumption that \(q\) contains \(2\) also covers the borderline possibility \(M=2\). Thus the maximum of \(v\) is \(M-1\). We show that \(v\) contains every value from \(1\) through \(M-1\). For \(k=1\), the assumed occurrence of \(2\) in \(q\) becomes an occurrence of \(1\) in \(v\). For \(2\le k\le M-1\), the value \(k+1\) lies between \(3\) and \(M\). It occurs somewhere in \(x\) by the covering condition, and it cannot occur in the suffix \((1,2)\), so it occurs in \(q\); after subtracting \(1\), it gives an occurrence of \(k\) in \(v\). All non-adjacent inequalities in \(v\) follow from those in the prefix \(q\), since subtracting a constant preserves inequalities. Hence \(v\in B_{N-2}\), and
\[
 x=C(v).
\]

Finally, suppose that \(q\) does not contain a \(2\). Since all entries of \(q\) are at least \(2\), they are then all at least \(3\). Define
\[
 v=(x_1-2,\ldots,x_{N-2}-2).
\]
This sequence is positive. Again let \(M\) be the maximum of \(x\). Since \(q\) is nonempty when \(N\ge3\) and all its entries are at least \(3\), the maximum lies in \(q\), and the maximum of \(v\) is \(M-2\). For each \(k\) with \(1\le k\le M-2\), the value \(k+2\) belongs to \(\{3,\ldots,M\}\). The covering condition gives an occurrence of \(k+2\) in \(x\), and this occurrence cannot lie in the suffix \((1,2)\); therefore it lies in \(q\) and becomes an occurrence of \(k\) in \(v\). The weak inequalities are once more preserved under a uniform subtraction. Thus \(v\in B_{N-2}\), and
\[
 x=D(v).
\]

The last two subcases are disjoint. In the image of \(C\), the prefix before \((1,2)\) contains a \(2\), because the admissible source contains a \(1\), which becomes \(2\) after adding \(1\). In the image of \(D\), every entry of that prefix is at least \(3\). They are also disjoint from the images of \(A\) and \(B\), because sequences in the first two images end in \(1\), whereas sequences in the last two images end in \(2\).

We have therefore established the disjoint decomposition
\[
 B_N=A(B_{N-1})\;\sqcup\;B(B_{N-1})\;\sqcup\;C(B_{N-2})\;\sqcup\;D(B_{N-2}).
\]
Since all four maps are injective, taking cardinalities yields
\[
 b_N=b_{N-1}+b_{N-1}+b_{N-2}+b_{N-2}
     =2b_{N-1}+2b_{N-2},
\]
which is (1).

It remains to identify this recurrence with A028859. Let \(a(n)\) be A028859, characterized by
\[
 a(0)=1,\qquad a(1)=3,\qquad
 a(n+2)=2a(n+1)+2a(n)\quad(n\ge0). \tag{6}
\]
For completeness, these are also exactly the counts of ternary strings of length \(n\) with no two consecutive zeros. There is one empty string and three strings of length one. For a valid ternary string of length \(n\ge2\), either its final symbol is \(1\) or \(2\), giving two choices appended to any valid string of length \(n-1\), or its final symbol is \(0\), in which case its preceding symbol must be \(1\) or \(2\), giving two choices for a suffix of the form \(10\) or \(20\) appended to any valid string of length \(n-2\). This gives precisely recurrence (6).

Now compare (1) and (6). We have
\[
 b_1=1=a(0),\qquad b_2=3=a(1).
\]
An induction on \(N\), using the common recurrence, gives
\[
 b_N=a(N-1)\qquad(N\ge1).
\]
Indeed, the assertion holds for \(N=1,2\); and if it holds for \(N-1\) and \(N-2\), then
\[
 b_N=2b_{N-1}+2b_{N-2}
     =2a(N-2)+2a(N-3)
     =a(N-1).
\]
Taking \(N=n+1\), we conclude that for every \(n\ge0\),
\[
 a(n)=b_{n+1}.
\]
Thus \(a(n)\) is exactly the number of length-\(n+1\) sequences of positive integers that cover an initial interval of positive integers and whose non-adjacent parts are weakly decreasing, as claimed.
